justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a gradually appreciating asset or index starting near 92.1 and drifting upward to 94.5 over the month. At the one-day horizon, the estimate of 92.1 is anchored closely to the most recent observed price or level, with only minimal expected drift — this is typical of mean-reversion assumptions in the short run combined with whatever modest directional momentum was present in the data at the time of the forecast. At the one-week horizon, the slight upward nudge to 92.8 reflects a mild bullish bias, perhaps from trend-following signals or a positive macro backdrop. By one month, the 94.5 estimate extrapolates that trend further, suggesting a roughly 2–3% appreciation over the period, which is consistent with moderate optimism but not an aggressive bull case.

The confidence interval widths widen substantially as the horizon extends, which is the natural consequence of uncertainty compounding over time. At one day, the 90% interval spans only about 5.2 units, reflecting high short-term predictability and low realized volatility in the near term. By one week, the interval opens to roughly 10.6 units, capturing the possibility of meaningful news events, technical breaks, or sentiment shifts within a week. At one month, the interval stretches to 23 units, acknowledging that over four weeks, macroeconomic data releases, central bank decisions, geopolitical developments, and earnings or policy surprises can all accumulate into large directional moves in either direction.

Specific risks that could push outcomes outside even the wide one-month interval include a sudden macroeconomic shock such as an unexpected recession signal, a major geopolitical escalation, or a surprise central bank policy pivot that dramatically reprices risk assets. On the upside, an unexpectedly strong economic data print or a resolution of an ongoing geopolitical or trade tension could produce a sharper rally than the upper bound anticipates. Liquidity crises or flash crashes, while rare, are also tail risks that confidence intervals built on historical volatility tend to underweight, meaning true tail outcomes may be fatter than the stated 90% range implies.
